text:
A simple artificial intelligence model achieves top-tier results in understanding human language tasks like sentiment analysis [P1_p1_c02]. 

Deep learning systems have already achieved great success in computer vision and speech recognition [P1_p1_c03]. Adapting these techniques for written text often involves converting words into vector representations, which are dense lists of numbers that capture semantic meaning [P1_p1_c03]. 

The new research explores a simple convolutional neural network built on top of pre-trained word vectors [P1_p1_c02, P1_p5_c04]. Originally invented for computer vision, these networks use filters to scan local features in data [P1_p1_c03]. In this model, the network scans windows of words in a sentence to extract key features [P1_p2_c01]. 

The key finding is that a straightforward model using pre-trained word vectors performs remarkably well across multiple benchmarks [P1_p1_c02, P1_p4_c03]. It competes strongly against much more complex deep learning models that require parse trees or intricate pooling schemes [P1_p4_c03]. Furthermore, fine-tuning those word vectors specifically for individual tasks delivers even greater performance gains [P1_p1_c02, P1_p4_c03]. The models improved upon the state of the art on four out of seven tasks, including sentiment analysis and question classification [P1_p1_c02]. 

This matters because it shows that pre-trained word vectors act as powerful universal feature extractors that can be easily and effectively utilized across different datasets [P1_p4_c03].
